messages.subject: [statnet_help] Network size limitations of ntelm and netlogit
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Network size limitations of ntelm and netlogit
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to run netlogit on networks of about 60,000 nodes, and I would
like to know if the SNA regression functions are designed to support such
large operations. I know, for instance, that with RSiena we are not
supposed to go further than a few hundred nodes for the algorithms to
converge in a reasonable time. But is this the case with SNA's regression
models as well?

My initial experience is negative: When I run the commands on my networks,
the R process expands in memory until it fills both the live memory and the
virtual memory and then it crashes (even with a single repetition). I
wonder if this is simply a matter of throwing more resource at R, and is
there a good way to calculate how much? Or are the current MRQAP algorithms
simply not adapted to larger networks?

Best,
Mahmood S. Zargar
PhD Candidate
Desautels Faculty of Management
McGill University

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Network size limitations of ntelm and netlogit
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Mahmood -

At present, those functions make heavy use of adjacency representations 
for the underlying data, and hence do not scale to graphs with more than 
~40,000 or so nodes (give or take) - getting around this limit would 
require a very different implementation. (Generating sufficiently high 
quality random permutation vectors might also become a problem as N 
becomes large, since this is a known challenge for pseudorandom number 
generators.  However, I am not aware of anyone who has closely examined 
the issue in this context, so the impact on real-world performance is 
hard to assess.)  A sparse-data MRQAP implementation for very large 
graphs could certainly be written, but to make it practical one would 
need to use an ergm-like term system to calculate covariate values on 
the fly (since you don't want to store all N^2 values) and whatnot.  
Doable, but I don't know if anyone has done it.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Plotting valued dynamic network?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeff,

 >
 > This prints all “weight” values on 1->2 in period 1, creating
 > overlapping labels. So how do I show only the highest weight from each
 > period?


First,  in your example, by repeatedly added edges between the same 
tail,head pair of vertices, you are actually creating a multiplex 
network.  I'm not sure if this was your intention, but I don't see an 
easy way to collapse the labels for this case, since you would need to 
look up the 'edge' objects by their endpoints.  If that is what you need 
to do, let me know I'll figure out a way..

But assuming that this was not intended to be a multiplex network, you 
should use 'activate.edges' to add additional activity spells after the 
edge is created (either with add.edge or add.edges.active).

re-writing your example

net<-network.initialize(5)
add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=2, onset=1, terminus=1.5)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=1, terminus=1.5, e=1)
activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=1.5, terminus=1.7)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=1.5, terminus=1.7, e=1)
activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=1.7, terminus=4)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=1.7, terminus=4, e=1)
activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=4, terminus=5)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',3,onset=4, terminus=5, e=1)
add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=3, onset=2.1, terminus=2.2)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2.1,terminus=2.2, e=2)
add.edges.active(net, tail=3, head=4, onset=2, terminus=3)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2,terminus=3, e=3)
activate.edges(net, e=3, onset=3, terminus=4)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=3,terminus=4, e=3)
add.edges.active(net, tail=5, head=4, onset=3, terminus=5)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=3,terminus=5, e=3)

or in a slightly condensed form, do all the edge activation at the same time

net<-network.initialize(5)
add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=2, onset=c(1,1.5,1.7,4), 
terminus=c(1.5,1.7,4,5))
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=1, terminus=1.5, e=1)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=1.5, terminus=1.7, e=1)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=1.7, terminus=4, e=1)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',3,onset=4, terminus=5, e=1)
add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=3, onset=2.1, terminus=2.2)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2.1,terminus=2.2, e=2)
add.edges.active(net, tail=3, head=4, onset=c(2,3), terminus=c(3,4))
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2,terminus=3, e=3)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=3,terminus=4, e=3)
add.edges.active(net, tail=5, head=4, onset=3, terminus=5)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=3,terminus=5, e=4)

when set up this way, your plot command will give you a warning 
indicating that it couldn't figure out which value to use

 > plot(network.extract(net,onset=1,terminus=2, 
trim.spells=TRUE),main='at time 1',arrowhead.cex=2, displaylabels=TRUE, 
boxed.labels=TRUE, label.pos=5, 
edge.label=na.omit(get.edge.value.active(net, "weight", 
onset=1,terminus=2)))

Warning message:
In get.edge.value.active(net, "weight", onset = 1, terminus = 2) :
   Multiple attribute values matched query spell for attribute 
weight.active on some edges. Only earliest value used


if you just wanted the earliest or latest value you could avoid the 
warning by specifying a rule:

 > get.edge.value.active(net, "weight", onset=1,terminus=2,rule='latest')
[1]  4 NA NA NA

 > get.edge.value.active(net, "weight"onset=1,terminus=2,rule='earliest')
[1]  1 NA NA NA

you could also do this by using network.collapse instead of network.extract


However, since you want the label with the maximum value, you will have 
to process the TEA attribute directly yourself

get.edge.value.active(net, "weight",onset=1,terminus=2,return.tea = TRUE)

The first element of each TEA attribute is the list of values 
appropriate for the time range (second is spell matrix) so should work 
to set your edge.label equal to

sapply( 
get.edge.value.active(net,"weight",onset=1,terminus=2,return.tea = TRUE),
    function(e){
       max(unlist(e[[1]]))
})

[1]  4 NA NA NA


If you were doing this as part of ndtv animation, you would probably 
want to make use of 'functional' attribute forms so that the values 
would be recalculate for each slice

library(ndtv)

render.animation(net,
           main=function(onset,terminus){paste('at 
time',onset,'-',terminus)},
           arrowhead.cex=2,
           displaylabels=TRUE,
           boxed.labels=FALSE,
           label.pos=5,
           edge.label=function(net,onset,terminus){
 
sapply(get.edge.value.active(net,"weight",onset=onset,terminus=terminus,return.tea 
= TRUE),
                     function(e){
                        max(unlist(e[[1]]))
                     }
             )
           }
)
ani.replay()


let me know if that works!

best,
  -skye

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm: non-integer "receiver" target.stats
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Carlo,

I am not 100% certain whether this is what you want, but it's perfectly
legal to set target.stats to a fractional value, even if it's for
something like edge count or in-tie count. This is because the model is
not about a specific graph but about a *distribution* of graphs, and
specifying that the expected number of in-ties of the node in question
is to be 0.2 is perfectly sensible. Most graphs in that distribution
will give that node 0 in-ties; some will give 1; and a few will give 2
or more, but on average, it will be 0.2.

                        I hope this helps,
                        Pavel

P.S. Depending on your specific model, you might be able to make this
more explicit using the valued ERGM framework. There, you can, in fact,
say that the ties are binomial(n=100), and that the target.stat is 20.
One can also specify a continuous uniform reference measure between 0
and 1, and use a beta-distribution-like model to the same effect.
However, these approaches are not as well understood as binary ERGMs.

On Thu, 2015-04-30 at 10:33 +1000, martina morris wrote:
> Hi Carlo,
> 
> Unfortunately, receiver stats are not "ensembles" -- they are node 
> specific integer counts of ties.  If you combine other nodes into the 
> base, it can function as an ensemble for a target count.  So, if you put 5 
> nodes into the base, and have a target of 1 tie, each node would get your 
> 0.2 ties in expectation.  Alternatively, you might be able to set the coef 
> for this receiver node using an offset to achieve the desired tie 
> probability, but the value may be difficult to find given the correlation 
> with other terms in the model.
> 
> I'm replying to the list here in case someone else has a better idea.
> 
> best,
> mm
> 
> On Wed, 29 Apr 2015, Carlo Campajola wrote:
> 
> > 
> > It would imply that say on 100 sampled graphs from the resulting distribution, roughly 20
> > would have receiver=1 for that node and the remaining would have 0. In principle target.stats
> > should fix the ensemble averages, so even an integer-valued quantity might have non-integer
> > mean value.
> > 
> > Il 29/apr/2015 20:01, "martina morris" <morrism@u.washington.edu> ha scritto:
> >       And what does a value of 0.2 mean?  You say this is not a weighted graph (and
> >       receiver stats haven't been coded up for wtd graphs in any case).  So I'm not
> >       clear what a target value of 0.2 would imply.
> >
> >       On Wed, 29 Apr 2015, Carlo Campajola wrote:
> > 
> >
> >             Dear Martina,
> >             thanks for your reply. I want to enforce a value of 0.2 for just one
> >             node (so the term is

> >             rounded down to 0, which is not what I
> >             want. I guess it's because the ergm with target.stats actually
> >             produces a random network through SAN over
> >             which it runs the ergm fitting, and obviously that network has either
> >             receiver=0 or 1 since the graph is not
> >             weighted. Any way to solve the problem without having to do some

messages.body_plain:
Does STERGM handle valued networks? I don't see a response term in the
stergm command, so I assume no.

My actual outcome is binary and directed edges, but I am getting very
unclear on activating edges in the dynamic network. Example:

I have three nodes active for different times:
A: 0-30
B: 10-40
C: 20-50

By definition edges are only possible for the following times:
AB/BA: 10-30
AC/CA: 20-30
BC/CB: 20-30

Now suppose I have broken intervals in which an edge exists for AB: 11-18
and 23-25. But I have a time-varying dyadic predictor which exists for all
possible periods 10-30.

Do I :
(1) activate the edge for 10-30 and list an edge attribute with value 1 or
0 depending on the existence of the tie.
(2) activate the edge for 11-18 and 23-25 only, and list the dyadic
predictor as a network attribute somehow for each time period ?

Examples would help.
Thanks
Jeff Carnegie

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Errors returned on models run after updating ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hello Statnet!

I am running into some issues with inconsistent model runs between
different versions of the ergm package.  I ran a series of models on  a
couple of diffferent networks that converged over the last few weeks.
However, after updating to ergm version 3.2.4, running models with the same
specifications now yields error messages.  Here are the messages:

1)  *Excessive correlation among the statistics. Using a
no-crosscorrelation approximation.*

This error seems to be associated with models that include a large number
of terms(including a bunch of nodemix terms).

2)  *1: In .ergm.mvar.spec0(z) :  Excessive correlation among the
statistics. Using a no-crosscorrelation approximation.*

This error term seems to be associated with models run a large number of
missing links (coded as NAs).

Again, these models converged error-free while using an older version of
the ergm package, but return errors under the current version.  Can anyone
shed light on this issue?  What are the implications for the model results
generated using the previous versions of ergm?

Thanks,
Mateo


-- 
Matt Robbins
Ph.D. Candidate
Center for Environmental Policy and Behavior
<http://environmentalpolicy.ucdavis.edu/>
Department of Environmental Science and Policy
Graduate Group in Ecology
University of California, Davis
